guide.title: Opt-out handling
guide.subtitle: What happens after a recipient replies STOP
guide.excerpt: Opt-out is two halves: the suppression record, and the check that runs before a marketing message is handed to the provider. Both run through one shared normalization, which is the part that usually breaks.

p: A suppression record is written when a recipient asks to stop. The record belongs to a tenant, a channel and an address, and it is written idempotently: a repeated opt-out refreshes the existing record rather than creating a second one.

The check runs before a marketing message is handed to the provider. If the address is suppressed, the message is not sent and the outcome is recorded as suppressed rather than as a failure — it was never attempted, so counting it as a delivery failure would be wrong.

sections.h: Which replies count as an opt-out
p: The recognition list follows the North American carrier standard: STOP, STOPALL, UNSUBSCRIBE, CANCEL, END and QUIT. OPTOUT and OPT OUT are included as widely supported variants. Because the messages the platform sends are not always in English, the local-language equivalent that appears in its own opt-out footer is recognized as well — so a recipient who replies in the language they were written to is not left subscribed.

sections.h: The matching is exact, and that is deliberate
p: Before matching, the reply is normalized: case is folded and punctuation is collapsed to spaces. Matching then requires the whole normalized reply to equal a keyword. It is not a substring search.

Substring matching would classify a reply like "please do not stop the promotion" as an opt-out, silently ending the conversation with a customer who asked for the opposite. The cost of exact matching is that an unusual phrasing such as "STOP please" is not auto-recognized — that one goes to a human, and the console can add it to the suppression list by hand.

sections.h: Coming back: START, YES and UNSTOP
p: Opt-out is required to be reversible. START, YES and UNSTOP are treated as the reverse action: the suppression record for that address is deactivated and a confirmation is sent back.

The confirmation goes out as transactional rather than marketing traffic. That ordering matters: if the recipient is still suppressed at the moment the confirmation is composed, a marketing classification would be blocked by the very gate it is confirming.

sections.h: HELP is a separate branch, and it is always answered
p: Replies that ask for help are answered with an explanation, and that reply is sent even to an address that has already opted out. A recipient who asked to stop and then asked for help is still entitled to the help text.

sections.h: Two limits you should know about
list: Some provider-side opt-out handling is carrier-level. A reply to STOP may be handled by the carrier and never delivered to the platform as an inbound message at all. Where that is the case, the platform recognizes the traffic pattern and logs it distinctly rather than pretending it has handled something it never saw.

Deactivating a record is a database change, and it is not the same as being deliverable again. On some sender types the carrier may have blocked the number on its own side; restoring the record does not undo that, and the carrier has to release it.

sections.h: One normalization, used by both sides
p: The write path and the read path share the same address normalization. This is the detail that decides whether the feature works at all: if the record is written under one spelling of a number and the check queries another, the gate silently stops matching, nothing errors and nothing turns red, and the recipient keeps receiving messages they opted out of.
sections.scope: Suppression is implemented for the SMS channel and is the only channel where it is enforced today. Do not assume it carries across to email or WhatsApp.
